metadata.title: A systematic review of the use of log-based process data in computer-based assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a PRISMA-guided systematic review and does not analyze student microdata from TIMSS/PISA/PIAAC/NAEP or any other large-scale assessment. Because no original assessment dataset is used for estimation, there are no sampling weights, replicate weights, or PV-based scaling/combining steps to apply. The review instead synthesizes how prior empirical studies constructed and used log-based process indicators (time, count, sequence) and how those indicators were used to infer latent constructs at different evidence-centered design levels. Consequently, weighting guidance for complex survey design is not applicable to the review’s own analyses, though the included primary studies may have used such methods.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because this is a systematic review that does not estimate cognitive achievement scores from ILSA/PV-based outcomes. The review does not perform missing-data handling for student-level records; instead, it applies inclusion/exclusion criteria to published studies and summarizes their reported methods and constructs. Therefore, missing-data handling is not reported as an analytic step in the review itself.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Systematic review selection followed PRISMA. The authors searched multiple databases (Web of Science, ProQuest Education, Scopus, and EBSCO host databases including ERIC and others) using combinations of process-data terms (e.g., log files, clickstream, paradata, keystroke, response time, action sequence) and educational assessment terms (PISA, PIAAC, TIMSS, PIRLS, NAEP, and large-scale/summative/formative assessment). Inclusion required peer-reviewed English publications (journal articles, conference papers, book chapters, and books) with full text available. Exclusions: (1) studies that did not measure the test-taking process based on embedded assessments/tests (e.g., learning systems without embedded summative/formative assessment), (2) conceptual/theoretical/review studies without empirical log-data use (methodological papers with empirical evidence were allowed), (3) studies not using computer log data limited to mouse clicks, keystrokes, and timing data (excluding eye-tracking, think-aloud, textual chat, questionnaires/surveys, product data, and qualitative interview data), and (4) studies without full text. The review also included references from a prior review to broaden coverage, resulting in 330 included publications.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This PRISMA systematic review synthesizes how log-based process data are used in computer-based assessments, focusing on data-driven reasoning within an evidence-centered design perspective. Across 330 included peer-reviewed publications (searched in Nov 2022 and Mar 2024; records published through Dec 31, 2023), the review reports trends in adoption and summarizes common process indicators: time indicators (used in 82% of studies), count indicators (32%), and sequence indicators (25%), with the most common indicator usage being time-only (51%). It also categorizes how process indicators infer latent constructs into four inferential levels, with level 4 (36%) most prevalent, and notes that many level-4 studies focus on latent response speed via log-normal response time models. The review does not estimate predictive models or report ML performance metrics because it does not conduct original student-level analysis; instead, it aggregates reported constructs (e.g., cheating, rapid guessing, persistence, planning, speed, latent engagement) and discusses benefits, challenges, and recommendations, including validity grounding and fairness/bias concerns in advanced AI methods. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a systematic review rather than an empirical ML study. As a result, there is no student-level dataset, no country-level analytic sample, no PV-based achievement outcome, no missing-data imputation strategy for microdata, and no trained ML model with performance metrics. The review’s contribution is methodological synthesis (indicator types, inferential levels, and construct categories) rather than predictive estimation.
